items.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002
items.q: I spent the whole day in the studio with Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington or Fats Waller

ctx.x: Well I must admit that I look back on it with a good deal of satisfaction. I’ve been very fortunate because in this business in particular, a lot of the associations that you form, at least initially, are accidental as hell. If someone tells me that I have been helpful to this or that career that’s exactly the thing that I want to hear because I have always looked on the role of the producer in a very specific way. Now one of the hardest things, and I’ve been at it, I’m getting perilously close to my fiftieth…

with doing this. The only real serious variation is that I have — I used to say in recent years — but for a lot of years, a lot of my attention has been focused on reissues and obviously the procedures are a little different there. For the most part that makes it possible to get into cliches like well I spent the whole day in the studio with Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington or Fats Waller, and he didn’t give me a hard time. But that joke got busted about a year ago because one of my most recent reissue projects…

exactly how I learned to swim. And it was, I also will say that, I said it many years ago with what I have learned I would never entrust as valuable and volatile a commodity as Thelonious to anybody as totally ignorant and inexperienced as I was at the time. But fortunately one of the great advantages of that, well basically it’s a 1950s phenomenon primarily, it happened a little before that, it happened a little after that, but the idea of the jazz fan as self-made jazz record producer actually the art owes a…

items.q: And there was a project that he came up with and sake me to do almost immediately, which was a five C.D. Fats Waller package.

ctx.x: Well sometimes it’s hard for me to figure out what Orrin Keepnews has been doing. (Laughs) One of the things that I’ve done which, at the moment, is questionable in my mind as to whether it was a wise thing to be doing, but I have…All through my career I keep making noises about the importance to me of remaining as unaffiliated as possible. Actually, what had happened a few years before my previous interview, was that I had voluntarily, this is something you can’t imagine in the current situation, I voluntarily…

many years, so that in the year of 1980, which now sounds like a hell of a long time ago, and actually it was. What happened there was I left Fantasy and, as they say, it’s something that seems incredible and impossible in today’s world, but I voluntarily left. I was all the things that you want to get to be, I was running the new jazz program there and heavily involved in re-issue work. You know, it’s hard for me, even the language that I use then is hard to use again in absolutely today’s world. I made…

was the first multi-C.D. package that I did for Sony. It was the opening of that period; it was also the closing of that period. That was, among other things, the last major project that I did for them. Apparently, one of the things that you don’t have in your life when you are an independent producer, you don’t necessarily get sensible explanations, or any explanations at all for what and when they hire you to do a specific job. The period that we were coming out of, there had been a great deal of jazz re-issue…
